YouTube Crypto Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Investment Channels

A familiar YouTube channel can be hijacked or imitated to promote a fake crypto investment.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-08-06 · 8 min read

Quick answer: Treat a YouTube crypto investment stream as suspicious if it promises guaranteed returns, asks for crypto or a withdrawal fee, or links to an unverified platform. Do not rely on a tick, subscriber count or creation date: hijacked channels can keep them. Check the FCA, contact your bank, and report it.
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Use the right recovery route. Follow the payment, account and identity checklist; reporting differs in Scotland.

What a YouTube crypto scam looks like

YouTube crypto scams often start with a lookalike channel, a compromised channel that has been renamed, or a livestream using edited or deepfake footage of a celebrity or public figure. The stream may promise a giveaway, guaranteed returns or a limited-time investment opportunity. A link in the description or comments leads to a cloned platform that displays a convincing balance but is controlled by the scammer. For more on manipulated video, see our deepfake video scam guide.

Red flags that reveal a YouTube crypto scam

  • A channel uses a lookalike name, handle or branding, or an established channel suddenly changes topic. A hijacked channel can keep its original subscriber count, creation date and verification badge.
  • The video promises guaranteed returns, quick profits or to double your money — no investment can guarantee that.
  • You are told to send money or cryptocurrency to an external website or wallet address.
  • Comments are disabled, or visible comments contain coordinated praise and screenshots of supposed profits. Treat this as context, not proof.
  • The message creates urgency with phrases such as 'limited time only', 'act now' or 'spots filling up fast'.
  • The linked website has a different or lookalike URL, including a changed spelling, hyphen or domain ending.
  • A site asks for a withdrawal tax, release fee, private key, seed phrase or account password. A legitimate exchange may ask for identity documents as part of KYC; ID by itself is not proof of a scam.

How the scam unfolds from first click to money loss

These scams often use a hijacked high-subscriber channel or a convincing lookalike. Old videos may be deleted and the channel renamed; a deepfake of a founder or celebrity is then streamed to an audience that trusts the account. The video sends viewers to a fake exchange or investment dashboard. After a bank-transfer, card or crypto deposit, the balance is fabricated. A withdrawal request triggers a tax or verification fee, and the site then disappears or keeps demanding money. Personal details supplied during sign-up may be reused in identity-theft or recovery scams.

How to verify if a YouTube crypto channel is genuine

Before clicking or paying, compare the channel name and handle with the creator's own website and independently found social accounts. A YouTube verification badge can help identify an official channel, but it is not proof that a promoted investment is genuine; a missing badge is not proof of a scam. Check whether the channel's recent content and any investment claim match the creator's official channels. Treat subscriber count and creation date as context only because a hijacked channel can retain both.

Check the investment firm in the FCA Firm Checker (https://www.fca.org.uk/consumers/fca-firm-checker), the Financial Services Register (https://register.fca.org.uk/) and the FCA Warning List (https://www.fca.org.uk/consumers/warning-list-unauthorised-firms). UK cryptoasset promotions to consumers must be made through an authorised or registered firm, or approved by an authorised firm, and must be clear, fair and not misleading with prominent risk warnings. That still does not make an investment safe. For a second opinion, compare the platform with our fake crypto exchange guide and crypto investment protection guide.

What to do immediately if you have already sent money

Stop contact and send no more money. Contact your bank or card issuer immediately using details you find independently. For an eligible UK Faster Payment or CHAPS transfer made on or after 7 October 2024, ask the bank to assess an APP-fraud reimbursement claim. The rules can cover eligible individuals, microenterprises and charities up to £85,000; a firm may apply an excess of up to £100, but not to a vulnerable consumer, and claims normally have a 13-month outer reporting limit.

Payments to a crypto exchange and same-provider or 'on-us' payments are treated differently, so do not assume mandatory reimbursement applies. If you paid by card, ask about chargeback; for a credit-card purchase costing more than £100 and no more than £30,000, ask whether Section 75 applies.

If you sent cryptocurrency, report the receiving exchange or wallet address and do not pay a recovery service. Change reused passwords, secure your email and YouTube accounts with two-step verification, and keep screenshots. If identity details were exposed, monitor your credit files through the three main agencies — Experian, Equifax and TransUnion — and any other agency holding a report, such as Crediva. Consider Cifas Protective Registration: it places a warning flag against your name and personal details in Cifas's National Fraud Database, is not insurance against losses, and costs £30 for two years.

Read our crypto recovery scam guide if someone later offers to recover your money for a fee.

How to report YouTube crypto scams in the UK

Report the fake video, channel or comment to YouTube using its report controls. Report the scam website to the NCSC through the Suspicious Website Reporting Service at https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/section/about-this-website/report-scam-website; forward a suspicious email to report@phishing.gov.uk only when the artefact is an email. If you lost money, report it to Report Fraud at reportfraud.police.uk or 0300 123 2040 in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland. Report the promotion or unauthorised firm to the FCA on 0800 111 6768 and use its Firm Checker and Warning List.

For consumer advice, use Citizens Advice in England and Wales, Advice Direct Scotland in Scotland, or Consumerline in Northern Ireland. Tell the receiving exchange or wallet provider about the transaction and preserve the wallet address, transaction ID, URLs and screenshots. Protecting yourself from YouTube crypto scams going forward

Be sceptical of any unsolicited YouTube investment promotion, especially one promising guaranteed or unusually high returns. Verify through the creator's own channels and the FCA's records rather than the link in the video. Never share a private key, seed phrase or password. Turn on two-step verification for YouTube, email and exchange accounts. A familiar channel can be hijacked, and deepfake video can make a false endorsement look convincing; see the deepfake video scam guide. If a supposed recovery expert contacts you after a loss, do not pay — read the crypto recovery scam guide.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell if a YouTube channel is really run by the crypto expert I think it is?

Do not use a tick as your deciding test. Compare the channel name and handle with the creator's own website and independently found social accounts. A verified badge is not proof of a genuine investment promotion, and a hijacked channel can retain its badge, subscriber count and creation date. Check the platform in the FCA Firm Checker and Warning List before paying.

I clicked a link from a YouTube video and deposited £500 to a crypto investment site. Can I get my money back?

Contact your bank immediately and ask it to treat the payment as an APP scam if it was a UK Faster Payment or CHAPS transfer on or after 7 October 2024; eligibility, limits and exclusions apply, and crypto-exchange and on-us payments are treated differently. Ask a card issuer about chargeback and Section 75 where relevant. Crypto transfers are difficult to reverse: report the exchange, wallet address and transaction ID to the provider and Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland.

What should I do if I see a YouTube comment promoting a crypto investment with a link?

Do not click the link. Instead, report the comment to YouTube by clicking the three-dot menu next to it and selecting 'Report comment' — describe it as spam or scam. If the comment is on a video by a real creator, let them know through independently found official channels, as they may not be aware of the impersonation.

Is it safe to use a cryptocurrency exchange that is advertised on YouTube?

An established exchange can advertise on YouTube, so an advert alone is not proof of fraud. Do not trust the video or comments as endorsement. Find the firm's website independently, check the FCA Firm Checker, Financial Services Register and Warning List, and check that any UK-facing crypto promotion meets the FCA's financial-promotion rules and risk-warning requirements. If the platform is missing, mismatched or promises guaranteed returns, do not deposit.

I provided my passport number and email to a fake investment site. What should I do?

Change your email password and enable two-step verification. Keep evidence, report the scam to Report Fraud (0300 123 2040) in England, Wales or Northern Ireland, or Police Scotland on 101 in Scotland, and tell the receiving exchange or wallet provider. Monitor your credit files through Experian, Equifax and TransUnion as the three main agencies, plus any other agency that holds a report, such as Crediva. If your identity is at heightened risk, Cifas Protective Registration places a warning marker in its National Fraud Database and costs £30 for two years.

Is identity verification itself a sign that a crypto platform is fake?

No. UK crypto firms may need identity checks under anti-money-laundering rules, and a genuine platform can ask for a passport or driving licence. Do not upload documents through a link in a YouTube video; find the platform independently, check FCA records, and treat any withdrawal fee, tax, seed-phrase or password request as a red flag.
